solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Knight has king in for wallop

indicators.note: to have something in is to hold it inside, so the king sits within the knight word

blocks.note: to dub someone is to make them a knight
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A knight with the king beside him is ready to give someone a beating.
explanation.definitionFit: To drub is to beat or thrash soundly, the same violent sense as giving a wallop.

clue.text: Graze by the sound of it in northern pastures

indicators.note: by the sound of it means we go on how the word is spoken

blocks.note: to rake is to scrape or graze the skin

explanation.surface: Animals grazing in the pastures of the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Graze' suggests cattle feeding, but it means scrape.
explanation.definitionFit: A raik is a Scots word for a range or pasture where animals roam.

clue.text: What commuter catches in the morning, leaning back (first off) having caught elevated railroad

definitions.text: What commuter catches in the morning

indicators.note: first off means the opening letter is removed
having caught means holding something inside

blocks.note: supine means lying or leaning on one's back
the L (or El) is Chicago's elevated railway

explanation.surface: A commuter on the morning train, leaning back on a raised railway.
explanation.walkthrough: SUPINE minus S gives UPINE, which takes in L.
explanation.definitionFit: The up line is the track carrying trains towards the city or major terminus, the one commuters take in the morning.

clue.text: Nasty Aussie insect turned up entirely in belly (7, two words)

indicators.note: in a down entry, turned up means read from bottom to top
in places the turned word inside the next

blocks.note: all means entirely
the bunt is the bellying part of a sail or net

explanation.surface: A vicious Australian insect turns up right inside someone's stomach.
explanation.definitionFit: The bull ant is a large Australian ant with a painful sting, so a nasty insect.

clue.text: Strong drink? After school dozes, having imbibed pastis (not wines)

indicators.note: 'not' tells us to take the named letters away from the word before it
to imbibe is to take in, so the sleeping word swallows the remnant

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for school
naps are short sleeps
the aniseed spirit, taken as written
Asti is an Italian sparkling wine, so several are Astis

explanation.surface: A schoolchild dozing off after downing pastis needs something strong.
explanation.walkthrough: Asti is a sparkling Italian wine, so 'wines' is a plural taken away letter for letter from the spirit, leaving a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Schnapps is a potent distilled spirit, so it is literally a strong drink; the question mark flags the playful phrasing.

clue.text: Many pets love this – cover the top of round tin that’s damaged

indicators.note: something damaged is bent out of shape, so the letters are rearranged
round means surrounding, so the covering word goes about the rest

blocks.note: to cap is to cover the top of something
taken as written, for rearranging

explanation.surface: Pet owners are told to put a lid on a dented tin.
explanation.definitionFit: Catnip is a herb whose scent cats find irresistible, hence loved by many pets.

clue.text: Former land-tax kept under wraps a long time

blocks.note: hid means concealed
an age is a long time

explanation.surface: An old property tax was concealed for ages.
explanation.definitionFit: Hidage was a tax levied in medieval England on each hide, a measure of land.

clue.text: Tally about right, slightly off

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the crooked word goes round the letter

blocks.note: agee is Scots for off the straight, awry
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A count that is almost correct but a little out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tally' looks like a noun but works as the verb meaning correspond.
explanation.definitionFit: To tally is to correspond or match, which is to agree.

clue.text: Former idol, a divinity, put in personal appearance

indicators.note: put in places the first pieces inside the last

blocks.note: PA is the abbreviation for personal appearance
taken as written
a god is a divinity

explanation.surface: A one-time pop idol, worshipped like a god, makes a personal appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former idol' suggests a faded celebrity, but means an idol in an obsolete sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Pagoda once also meant an idol or image of a deity in an Eastern temple, an obsolete sense.

clue.text: Mantle, eastern, in puckered fabric

indicators.note: in places the compass letter inside the fabric

blocks.note: plissé is cloth with a puckered or crinkled finish
E for eastern

explanation.surface: A cloak of eastern style made from crinkled cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A pelisse is a long cloak or fur-lined coat, a mantle in the sense of an outer garment.

clue.text: Cover for pair of GIs in camp the rest lent out (11, two words)

definitions.text: Cover for pair of GIs in camp

indicators.note: out means disordered, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the eleven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Two soldiers in camp borrow cover while everyone else lends theirs.
explanation.definitionFit: A shelter tent is the small two-man pup tent issued to US soldiers, each carrying half.

clue.text: Nut tree, source of a cup Asia fashioned

indicators.note: something fashioned has been shaped anew, so these letters are reworked

blocks.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A tree whose fruit can be made into an Asian-style cup.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is apt: the sapucaia's large woody fruit, the monkey pot, can serve as a cup.
explanation.definitionFit: The sapucaia is a South American tree that bears edible paradise nuts, related to the Brazil nut.

clue.text: Flax-cutter’s tool, form of wand English waved

indicators.note: form of means a new shape, so the letters are reshaped
waved means swung about, so the letters are moved around

blocks.note: the eleven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An English wand swung about to process flax.
explanation.definitionFit: A swinglehand is a wooden blade used to beat flax and separate the fibres from the woody parts.

clue.text: Wader feeble, ailing internally

indicators.note: internally places the second word inside the first

blocks.note: wet means weak or ineffectual
ill means sick

explanation.surface: A wading bird is weak and sick inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The willet is a large North American shorebird, one of the sandpiper family of waders.

clue.text: Writer’s hollow task, article for the French

blocks.note: darg is a Scots and northern word for a day's work or task
le is a French definite article

explanation.surface: An author's empty chore, with a French article thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: The writer is Sir Walter Scott, who used dargle for a dell; 'hollow' looks like an adjective for 'task' but is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A dargle is a wooded dell or small valley, a word recorded from Scott's writing.

clue.text: Almost bare in earth? Treatment with this is useless

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
in places the shortened word inside the next one

blocks.note: naked means bare
soil is earth

explanation.surface: Burying something nearly naked in the ground does no good at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole sentence describing the remedy rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Snake oil is a quack remedy sold as a cure-all, so treatment with it achieves nothing.

clue.text: Number attached to England, wavering about independence, without agreeing

indicators.note: attached to says the first piece is joined directly onto what follows
wavering means unsteady, so the country's letters shift about

blocks.note: No. is the abbreviation for number
taken as written, for rearranging
I is the abbreviation for independence or independent

explanation.surface: A numbered team linked to England wobbles over going it alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' tells us the shuffled ENGLAND goes round I.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonaligned describes a state that has not signed up to either side, that is, one standing apart without agreement.

clue.text: That old-fashioned twinkle exhibited by man catching first sight of lass

indicators.note: first sight of means only the opening letter of the word is seen
catching means holding something, so the man word surrounds the letter

blocks.note: gent is short for gentleman
the opening letter of the girl

explanation.surface: A gleam in a man's eye on first spotting a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That old-fashioned' marks the answer as obsolete: glent is an old form of glint.
explanation.definitionFit: Glent is an archaic variant of glint, a brief flash or sparkle of light.

clue.text: Bowling ball, over almost attracting affection

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter goes
bowling means rolling along, so the letters tumble into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cricket delivery and an over draw fond attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowling ball' looks like one object but the first word is the anagram signal; OVER loses its R.
explanation.definitionFit: Lovable means easy to love, inspiring warm feeling or fondness.

clue.text: Seek help with engraving

blocks.note: first meaning: to pursue or go after
second meaning: to decorate metal by engraving or embossing

explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks for help in finding an engraver; the two parts are separate senses of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Chasing is the metalworker's craft of tooling patterns into a surface, while to chase also means to pursue.

clue.text: Trace rigidity without inner depth

indicators.note: without inner means lacking a letter from the middle

blocks.note: hardness is stiffness
d is the abbreviation for depth

explanation.surface: Detecting stiffness with no deep interior.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trace' reads as a verb but is the noun: a strap of a horse's tack.
explanation.definitionFit: Traces are the straps by which a horse pulls a cart, part of its harness, so one stands for the whole here.

clue.text: Set free once, so let out

indicators.note: out here means disordered, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the five letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone freed in the past is released again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'let out' reads as 'released', echoing the definition, but 'let' belongs to the letters being rearranged and only 'out' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Loste is an obsolete (Spenserian) past participle of loose, meaning released.

clue.text: Old helmet to recognize when lifted

indicators.note: in a down clue lifted means the letters read upwards

blocks.note: to tell is to distinguish or recognise
as means when, as in 'as he arrived'

explanation.surface: A knight identifies an antique helmet when it is raised.
explanation.definitionFit: A sallet is a fifteenth-century light helmet with a flared back, a piece of medieval armour.

clue.text: The lady’s upset for this reason? No longer

blocks.note: her is the possessive for a woman
to eat is to worry or trouble, as in what's eating you

explanation.surface: Asking why a woman is distressed, and saying she is over it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' looks like an anagram signal but means EAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Hereat is an archaic adverb meaning because of this, so 'No longer' marks it as obsolete.

clue.text: ‘Carry-on’ woman with chaps endlessly is responsible for such a caper

indicators.note: endlessly means without the ending, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: Carry On Cleo is a 1964 British film comedy in the Carry On series
chaps are men

explanation.surface: A woman from a comedy film and her men cause some lively antics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caper' suggests a romp, but it is the plant; the Carry On films are a long-running series of British comedy films.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleome, the spider flower, belongs to the caper family of plants.

clue.text: Drum, one of a pair, is damaged? Could be ear skin

indicators.note: damaged means knocked out of shape, so the combined letters are scrambled

blocks.note: the letters that the scrambled combination could make
taken as written, the extra letters joined to the answer

explanation.surface: A broken drum might turn out to be an eardrum.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the answer plus IS, damaged, could be EAR SKIN; so remove IS from the letters of EARSKIN to leave NAKER.
explanation.definitionFit: A naker is a medieval kettledrum, played in pairs like modern timpani.

clue.text: A ‘K’ a Singh’s deployed … is this?

definitions.text: A ‘K’ a Singh’s deployed … is this?

indicators.note: deployed means spread out and arranged, so the letters are redistributed

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
taken as written, the letters left over

explanation.surface: Asking whether a Sikh's item is one of his Ks.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the answer plus IS makes A K A SINGH, so IS is removed. The whole clue also defines: the kangha is one of the five Ks a Sikh wears.
explanation.definitionFit: The kangha is the wooden comb, one of the five articles of faith beginning with K that initiated Sikhs carry.

clue.text: Earl unhappily admitted stress getting faster

indicators.note: unhappily suggests things going awry, so the nobleman's letters are disturbed
admitted means let in, so the shuffled title goes inside the stress word

blocks.note: accent is emphasis or stress in speech
taken as written, for rearranging

explanation.surface: A miserable earl let in strain and found himself speeding up.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective accelerant means accelerating, causing things to go more quickly.

clue.text: Call from a poet arrived with Latin in

indicators.note: with something in means holding it inside

blocks.note: came means arrived
L for Latin

explanation.surface: A poet's summons came with some Latin in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Clame is Spenser's spelling of claim, used in the old sense of to call or name.

clue.text: Whereon to park stetsons fixed there, the lot included? (8, two words)

indicators.note: fixed means rigged or rearranged, so the letters are reworked
included places the second element inside the first

blocks.note: taken as written, for rearranging
the lot means everything

explanation.surface: Asking where cowboys' hats get hung, all of them fixed in place.
explanation.walkthrough: Stetsons are cowboy hats, hinting at the American term for the furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: A hall tree is the North American name for a hallstand, a pole with hooks for coats and hats.

clue.text: What may accompany bill topping millions? It’s grimy

indicators.note: in a down entry, topping means sitting above, so the first piece comes before the second

blocks.note: bill and coo is an idiom for lovers' whispering
M is the abbreviation for millions

explanation.surface: Something that goes with a large bill on top of millions is dirty business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bill' suggests money, but it is the bird's beak in 'bill and coo'; 'topping' puts that piece above M in a down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Coom is coal dust, soot or grimy refuse, the stuff that makes things grimy.

clue.text: Surgically remove bit of lump to nullify circles

indicators.note: bit of means just a small piece, here the opening letter
circles means surrounds, so the nullifying word goes round the letter

blocks.note: in law to abate a writ is to nullify it
first letter of the lump

explanation.surface: A surgeon cuts away part of a lump to neutralise it.
explanation.definitionFit: To ablate is the medical term for removing tissue, often by excision or vaporising.

clue.text: State about to welcome European artist

indicators.note: to welcome is to take in, so the first word wraps round the painter

blocks.note: on means concerning or about
Paula Rego, the Portuguese-born painter

explanation.surface: A country is about to receive a painter from Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to' reads as 'soon going to', but 'about' is the outer piece and 'to welcome' the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Oregon is one of the fifty United States, on the Pacific north-west coast.

clue.text: Depots currently fashionable offering protection for banks

blocks.note: camps are bases or stations
hot means in vogue right now

explanation.surface: Trendy warehouses provide security for financial institutions.
explanation.walkthrough: The banks are riverbanks, not financial ones.
explanation.definitionFit: A campshot is a facing of piles and boards along a river bank to guard it against erosion.

clue.text: With tons etc crookedly caught in the act, spotted by the police?

indicators.note: crookedly means out of line, so these letters are bent into a new order
caught in places the shuffled letters inside the following word

blocks.note: a deed is an act
t is the abbreviation for ton or tons
taken as written, for rearranging

explanation.surface: A crook caught red-handed with tons of goods is spotted by officers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught in the act' reads as one idiom for being found out, but splits into 'caught in' and 'the act'.
explanation.definitionFit: Detected means discovered or found out, which is what police do to criminals; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Title of distinguished Japanese book, short one

indicators.note: short means cut down, so the biblical name loses its ending

blocks.note: Samuel is a book of the Old Testament
a means one

explanation.surface: The honorific given to a celebrated Japanese author, in short.
explanation.definitionFit: Sama is a Japanese honorific suffix showing high respect, more formal than san.
